source: Guo, Du, Chen, Chang, Wang (2026) CASCADE: Case-Based Continual Adaptation for LLMs During Deployment
finding: CASCADE keeps one rule: a new case (query, answer, reward) is stored only if the binary reward is 1. Failed attempts leave the case bank unchanged.
numbers: 16 tasks (DTLBench plus ALFWorld, web search, tool use, MIMIC); macro success +20.9% over zero-shot; 5 seeds; backbone mostly Qwen3-32B
quote: If the generated solution is effective (i.e., rt = 1), CASCADE retains the new case
limits: Retention is not ablated. The retention rule is fixed (success only); no variant stores failures, dedups or forgets.
agent_relevance: This is our S9 baseline: store a case only after a checked pass. It is the simplest policy and has no store-all comparison.

source: Guo et al. (2026) CASCADE, limitations section
finding: The authors say their own retention is incomplete: it drops failed attempts that may hold information, and long-horizon memory growth, case management and forgetting are untested.
numbers: No figures; stated as limitations.
quote: learns from successful experiences, discarding failed attempts that may contain informative signals
limits: Authors' admission, not a measurement.
agent_relevance: The paper that names this subfield has no evidence on pruning or on keeping traps. We cannot cite it for those.

source: Guo et al. (2026) CASCADE, theory section and Supplementary C.5 (human-in-the-loop)
finding: Theory: the coverage gap (no relevant past case exists) shrinks sub-linearly as successful cases accumulate, if similar queries recur and the base model has non-zero success chance. When humans fix answers so every case can be stored (p_min=1), most tasks improve, but four tasks got worse.
numbers: Deterioration seen on MIMIC-MR, MIMIC-MSR, CMDL and LFD when storing the ground-truth case every step; CASCADE still beat NP-CBR in all settings.
quote: retriever policies of NP-CBR and CASCADE struggle to manage the growing and diverse case bank
limits: Within limited online timesteps; retriever, not retention, is blamed. Theory needs the three stated conditions.
agent_relevance: Storing more correct cases can hurt when retrieval cannot sort a bigger bank. Retention and retrieval must be tuned together.

source: Guo et al. (2026) CASCADE main results (Fig. 3) and ablations
finding: Learning which stored case to retrieve (bandit) adds only a few points over plain similarity retrieval on the same success-only bank. A success-only case bank can beat gradient training.
numbers: NP-CBR 63.76% to CASCADE 66.68% average; CASCADE beats REINFORCE+LoRA on 9 of 12 tasks with <4 GB GPU memory; with 4 retrieved cases it beats it on all 12.
limits: Qwen3-32B headline; other sizes in appendix. Ablations vary retriever, not what is retained.
agent_relevance: Most of the gain comes from storing verified successes at all (NP-CBR already large), not from clever policy. Cheap retention is a strong default.

source: Xiong, Lin, Xie, He, Liu, Tang, Lakkaraju, Xiang (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: Experience-Following Behavior
finding: Direct test of retention policy. Four agents (RegAgent, EHRAgent, AgentDriver, CIC-IoT) compared under: fixed memory, add-all, three automatic LLM-judge filters (C1-C3), and a strict oracle filter. Add-all and weak filters gave flat or falling success over time. The strict filter kept improving.
numbers: 5 evaluators x 4 agents; C3 = GPT-4.1-mini fine-tuned on only 300 judged trajectories, which already beat C1/C2 and add-all. Fixed memory sometimes beat noisy-filter runs.
quote: indiscriminate memory addition will easily introduce incorrect executions for the agent to learn from
limits: Strict evaluator is ground truth, not available online. Exact table values were not parseable from the PDF text; trends read from text and figure captions.
agent_relevance: Store only what a trusted check passes. A weak self-judge as the gate can be worse than freezing memory. This supports G3 and G2 for S9.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) experience-following property
finding: Agents copy retrieved cases: the more similar the new input is to a stored input, the more similar the output is to the stored output. This holds across GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3.
numbers: On synthetic RegAgent with a large bank, Pearson r near 1 between input and output similarity; lower under fixed small memory where the model reasons more.
limits: Measured as embedding similarity of outputs, not correctness.
agent_relevance: A stored case is a strong prior. Every stored error will be replayed on near neighbours, so retention quality matters more than quantity.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) error propagation
finding: A wrong stored case misleads later tasks, whose own wrong outputs are then stored, so errors compound. Even with human inspection some records have incorrect intermediate steps.
numbers: Measured against an error-free memory baseline built during execution (Sec 3.4, Appendix B.3); gap between agent and perfect-memory level shown in Fig. 4.
limits: Gap sizes are in figures; not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Store a trap label with a case if it ever failed on reuse; do not rely on the original pass alone.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) misaligned experience replay
finding: Some stored cases passed the quality filter yet hurt later tasks when retrieved (right answer for the wrong reason, or off-distribution). Later-use scores act as free quality labels for stored cases.
numbers: Retained records had lower error than deleted ones under strict evaluator (Fig. 6); lowest-utility record removed when bank is capped (100 records EHRAgent, 180 AgentDriver).
limits: Needs a reliable utility evaluator; with a noisy one, deletion helped one agent and hurt another.
agent_relevance: This is the harm case we need: track reuse outcome per case. Our own reuse counts and harm cases are the right signal for deletion.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) deletion strategies (Table 2, Fig. 5)
finding: Periodic deletion (every 500 steps, utility threshold) cut memory a lot for small performance loss. History-based deletion (drop a case after n retrievals with low average utility) helped with strict evaluator but was unstable with unfine-tuned LLM judges. Combined was best on size/performance balance.
numbers: RegAgent row (one setting): no deletion 63.18, periodic 60.88, history 62.10, combined 59.32 success. With strict judge on AgentDriver, history deletion beat the error-free-memory baseline. GPT-4o-mini as history judge helped EHRAgent but hurt AgentDriver.
limits: Row assignment to strategy inferred from text order; thresholds set per agent.
agent_relevance: Prune by observed reuse utility with a minimum-retrieval count, not by age alone. A noisy judge makes pruning risky.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory
finding: Counter-design to CASCADE: store distilled strategy items from both successes and failures, judged by the agent itself (LLM-as-judge) with no ground truth. Max 3 items per trajectory. Consolidation is minimal: items are appended with no pruning.
numbers: WebArena, Mind2Web, SWE-Bench-Verified; up to 20% relative gain and up to 16% fewer steps; WebArena up to 1.4 fewer steps than no memory, SWE-Bench-Verified 2.8 fewer
limits: Authors state they kept consolidation simple on purpose; no forgetting tested. Judge is the same backbone.
agent_relevance: Store a short lesson, not the raw trace. Failures can be stored if turned into a rule.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank, failure ablation (Fig. 7)
finding: Adding failed trajectories helps only if the memory format can use them. Success-only methods got worse or flat; ReasoningBank gained.
numbers: WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash: Synapse 40.6 to 41.7; AWM 44.4 to 42.2 (drop); ReasoningBank 46.5 to 49.7 with failures.
limits: One subset and backbone. No standard error given in text.
agent_relevance: Directly tests CASCADE's drop-failures rule: storing failures raw is neutral to harmful; storing them as lessons gives about +3 points.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank, judge-accuracy robustness
finding: Retention gate noise matters less than expected for strategy-level memory: success rates were similar across simulated judge accuracy of 70-90%, with ground-truth 100% best. Real Gemini-2.5-flash judge accuracy was 72.7%.
numbers: Judge accuracy simulated from 100% down to 50% (random). Baseline judge 72.7%.
quote: the judge's accuracy does not significantly impact the performance
limits: Contradicts Xiong et al. for instance-level memory; the difference may be abstraction level. At 50% the result degraded.
agent_relevance: A gate that stores abstract lessons tolerates a noisy check; a gate that stores raw cases does not. Test both for S9.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory (AWM)
finding: Online mode: an LM judge labels each test trajectory success or failure, and only judged successes are turned into reusable workflows and added to memory. Wrong workflows from wrong judgments degrade performance.
numbers: WebArena: +12.0 absolute points, +51.1% relative over BrowserGym baseline; Mind2Web online beats offline by more as domain gap widens; cross-task step SR gains 7.4-8.9, cross-website 3.6-3.8, cross-domain 14.0-16.9 points over MindAct
limits: GPT-4 backbone. Authors note online-induced workflows from model predictions are not always correct.
agent_relevance: Same success-only gate as CASCADE, at a coarser grain (workflow). Shows retention by judge works and its main failure is a false pass.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Long-term memory holds only distilled verbal reflections on failed trials, and the authors cap it to a small bounded set. A binary environment signal triggers a stored reflection.
numbers: Tested on 134 ALFWorld tasks, HotPotQA, HumanEval; ablation of the self-reflection step on HotPotQA CoT(GT)
limits: Memory is reset per task; it is not a cross-task case bank. Cap size not read from the extracted text.
agent_relevance: Opposite retention rule: store failures as lessons, bound the store. Useful for traps.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners
finding: Experience pool holds both successes and failures. Insights are kept in a list edited by ADD, EDIT, REMOVE, AGREE operators; successful trajectories are retrieved by task similarity. Gathering with retries (Reflexion) gave a more diverse pool than single-pass ReAct and better results.
numbers: HotpotQA / ALFWorld: insights-only 36% / 50%, retrieval-only 31% / 55%; retrieval by task similarity beat reason similarity, which beat random selection on ALFWorld (Table 3)
limits: Insight/retrieval figures read from text; GPT-3.5/4 backbones.
agent_relevance: Success/failure pairs for the same task carry the most information. Keep paired failures long enough to compare, then abstract them.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL ablation on insight extraction
finding: Adding self-reflections into the insight-extraction step hurt, because reflections sometimes hallucinate. Learned insights beat hand-crafted ones. A stronger model writes better insights.
numbers: HotpotQA ablation, Table 3 (exact values not extracted)
limits: Single environment for this ablation.
agent_relevance: Do not retain model-written reasons without a check; unverified reflections poison the store.

source: Suzgun, Yuksekgonul, Bianchi, Jurafsky, Zou (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet
finding: A curator model rewrites a compact cheatsheet after each query: keep useful, generalizable items, remove wrong or superseded ones. Appending the full history is worse than curating.
numbers: AIME 2024 Claude 3.5 Sonnet: baseline 23.3%, full-history 26.7%, DC 50.0%. GPT-4o AIME 2024: baseline 20.0%, full-history 6.7%, DC-RS 40.0%. Game of 24 GPT-4o 10% to 99%. GPQA-Diamond Claude 59.6% to 68.7%.
limits: Small test sets (30 AIME questions per year, so one question is 3.3 points). Gains tie to model capacity.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence against store-everything: uncurated history can fall below baseline.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet limitations
finding: Small models gain little or lose. Bad heuristics in memory are amplified in the same embedding neighbourhood. The curator sometimes writes 'previous content preserved' and so truncates memory.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini: DC-Cu and DC-RS fell below baseline on AIME 2024; Claude 3.5 Sonnet on Game of 24 only 12% to 14%; R1/o1 models showed minimal or inconsistent gains
quote: faulty heuristics that slip into memory can be equally amplified
limits: Qualitative statements for some items.
agent_relevance: Retention by model-curator needs a capable model and a diff check that old items were not silently dropped.

source: Evo-Memory (2025) Benchmarking LLM Agent Test-time Learning with Self-Evolving Memory
finding: Memory gains follow task similarity. An agent that prunes (ReMem: Think, Act, Refine with prune action) beat baselines that store everything. Naive accumulation of unfiltered failures degraded baselines.
numbers: Gain vs within-dataset similarity: Pearson 0.717 (Gemini 2.5 Flash), 0.563 (Claude 3.7 Sonnet). Pruning rate 36.8% on GPQA (diverse), 17.5% and 10.8% on AIME sets.
limits: Correlation across datasets, small number of points. Author list not recorded.
agent_relevance: Expect more redundancy to prune in diverse streams. Retention value depends on how often problems recur.

source: Evo-Memory (2025) Table 2 and Table 3
finding: Successful experiences from harder tasks transfer better than the reverse. When both successes and failures are stored on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, baselines drop; ReMem stays stable.
numbers: HardEasy order: up to 0.94 success / 0.97 progress for ReMem
limits: Only ALFWorld and ScienceWorld for the failure test.
agent_relevance: Prefer keeping solved hard cases; do not store raw failures without a filter.

source: Memento (2025) Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Memento's Write appends every finished case (state, action, reward), success or failure, once the task completes. A learned Q-function chooses which stored cases to use. Only the final step of a trajectory is stored to avoid redundant storage.
numbers: GAIA validation 87.88% after 3 iterations (memory built from scratch); GAIA test 79.40% using validation bank; DeepResearcher F1 66.6%; HLE 24.4% PM
limits: Planner GPT-4.1, executor o3. Leaderboard-style results, no retention ablation.
agent_relevance: The opposite of CASCADE: store everything, learn to retrieve. Compare the two on the same stream.

source: Memento (2025) K ablation (Table 3)
finding: A small, high-quality retrieved set beats a big one. Performance peaks at 4 retrieved cases and flattens or drops after.
numbers: DeepResearcher: K=4 best, F1 64.5, PM 78.5; K swept over 0, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32
quote: CBR benefits from a small, high-quality memory
limits: One dataset; memory content not varied.
agent_relevance: Bank size is not the constraint; shown cases per prompt is. Retain for coverage, retrieve few.

source: Chhikara et al. (2025) Mem0
finding: Dialogue memory with an explicit retention operator per new fact: ADD if nothing equivalent exists, UPDATE to merge, DELETE if contradicted, NOOP if redundant.
numbers: LOCOMO: J score 66.88% (Mem0) and 68.44% (Mem0g); response time 91% lower than full context; full context scores highest but costs more
limits: Conversation facts, not problem-solving cases. Judge is an LLM.
agent_relevance: Gives the four-way ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP rule we can run on case dedup, with a similarity search first.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager
finding: A skill enters the library only after it is generated, executed and passed by a self-verification check. If verification fails after 4 code rounds, nothing is stored and the curriculum picks another task.
numbers: Removing self-verification cut discovered items by 73% (largest drop among feedback types).
quote: Self-verification is the most important among all the feedback types.
limits: Minecraft; verifier sometimes misses success (spider string).
agent_relevance: The cleanest retention gate: execution plus verifier before write. False negatives cost a skill; false positives cost trust.

source: Smyth and Keane (1995) Remembering to forget: competence-preserving case deletion
finding: Classic CBR maintenance: delete cases by competence category (pivotal, spanning, support, auxiliary), removing auxiliary first, so coverage stays while the base shrinks. Not opened this session; cited from memory.
numbers: Not recorded; open the original before use.
limits: Pre-LLM, static classification case bases; not verified here.
agent_relevance: A ready deletion order for our bank: drop cases another case already solves, keep pivotal ones. Check against the case-base maintenance subfield (07).

source: Link to sibling subfields
finding: Retention overlaps with Case-base maintenance (07), Retrieval as a bandit (09), Relevance-based fate of memories, and Prioritised memory access. Not covered here.
limits: Note only. Web search quota was exhausted, so no forward-citation search was run.
agent_relevance: Pruning policy belongs to 07; here we only record which new cases are admitted.
